fact: DHIS2/HISP reports that the Unique Learner ID system is to be piloted in four districts, in at least 20 schools per district, before scaling to all public primary schools in the selected districts; no school is stated to be using it yet (no event date given; dated by publication).
The project's stated goal is a unique learner ID for every primary school student, with the pilot scaling to public primary schools (no event date given; dated by publication).

The Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education has launched a national initiative to build a learner-centred education data system on DHIS2, comprising a Unique Learner ID system and a national data hub (launch date not given; dated by publication).

The initiative is the Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education's, implemented by a consortium led by the HISP Centre at the University of Oslo with UNICEF supporting; national and district teams are to be trained as future custodians (dated by publication).
The project is funded by the Global Partnership for Education, with UNICEF supporting implementation; no domestic funding is stated (dated by publication).

The initiative sits within the 'Delivering the Foundations of Learning for All' programme (2024-2027) and is said to be aligned with the Education Sector Plan 2022-2026 and a forthcoming national EMIS policy (dated by publication).

The Data Landscapers 54-country review (an AI-assisted compilation, the author's own analysis) states that rural primary schools in Sierra Leone record attendance, enrolment and learning outcomes predominantly on paper registers and forms, that it found no routine digital tools at rural schools, and scores schools 1; it gives no date for the statement, so the document's published date is used.

fact: The Wi De Ya site states that school leaders use the app on a tablet to add profiles of individual learners and to record daily pupil attendance from the class register (and teacher attendance by fingerprint), the data syncing to an online database for the TSC and MBSSE when connected; dated to the rollout it says starts from March 2023.

The Wi De Ya site states that a rollout to 300 primary schools across all districts starts from March 2023, to be followed by planned rollouts to 1,500 and 4,000 schools with details to be confirmed; it gives no total of primary schools and no count of schools actually entering data.
The first rollout stage named is 300 primary schools, in government and government-assisted schools; later stages are given as school counts without a level.

Wi De Ya is led by the Teaching Service Commission in collaboration with the Ministry of Basic and Senior Secondary Education, and developed and tested by CGA Technologies (the page is undated; its published year is used).
Wi De Ya is funded by the Multi Donor Trust Fund (World Bank, GPE, EU, Irish Aid and FCDO); no domestic funding is stated (the page is undated; its published year is used).

CGA Technologies' project report says Wi De Ya had been rolled out to 300 primary schools so far in academic year 2022-23, and was designed to be usable in early childhood centres and secondary schools, where it was not yet in use.

The report says school leaders enter each learner's profile and daily learner attendance on the school's tablet, attendance being submitted at the end of the school day, with the data shown on dashboards for TSC and MBSSE; average learner attendance recorded was 80 per cent.

The report calls this the '300-school rollout phase': 300 purposely selected primary schools, each given a tablet and training; the count is of schools in the rollout, not of schools reporting, and it says learner attendance reporting rates varied by chiefdom and were lower in some rural ones, with no total of primary schools given.

The report says Wi De Ya was commissioned by the Teaching Service Commission in collaboration with MBSSE under the Free Education Project; CGA Technologies built it and managed the tablets, which MBSSE loaned, under TSC's leadership.
The report says Wi De Ya was funded by the Multi Donor Trust Fund of the World Bank, GPE, the EU, Irish Aid and FCDO, under the Free Education Project.
